prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have moved from B054 to B036 and I want to say plainly why. In round 1 I said I would take the lattice clock seriously if Kroll and Lindroth could show that the magic-wavelength idea is the decisive conceptual step, and they have done so. Lindroth explained that trapping many neutral atoms at a wavelength where the clock transition is not light-shifted removes the trade-off between atom number and motional and Doppler systematics, and neither the comb nor ion control contains that idea. Kroll added that the prize should be framed around the lattice concept so that it does not adjudicate lattice versus ion clocks. That answers my novelty objection well enough for me. What remains is a case with a stable interpretation, reproduction with Sr, Yb and Hg in laboratories on several continents, downstream reach in constants, redshift and geodesy, and a credit that maps onto two contributions: Katori for the concept and first lattice clocks, Ye for the record accuracy and systematics. A citation I could defend: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level. It leaves ion clocks, other lattice-clock groups and the SI redefinition outside the citation. I judge Ye's many-body and spin-exchange work to be a second storyline and would keep it out.
statement.case_against: This is still the most instrument-like achievement on the shortlist and it sits far from my own field, so I rely on colleagues for the atomic physics and I know that is a limit on my judgement. The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize is a risk of framing, and a citation drawn loosely could read as a second metrology prize for the same lineage. Credit at the margin is shared with Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and with ion-clock groups. Against my own earlier choice: B054 has a clean prediction-and-observation chain, but the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission cannot be repaired because Zhang is deceased, the 2016 overlap is real, and only one member ranked it first and four ranked it sixth or lower. I should not keep defending it on the strength of my own opening ballot.

responses.point: B036 rests on a conceptual step that neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 ion-control prize contains: neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, with the citation worded narrowly. Lindroth also pointed out that B054 has a contested HgTe prediction credit outside the three names.
responses.response: Your argument on the magic-wavelength condition is the one I asked for, and it is why I have moved. It separates the lattice clock from the comb and from single-ion control, which is where I thought the weakness was. Your note on B054 is also fair: the HgTe prediction credit is a gap I cannot close within three names. I part from you on one point. I would not put Ye's many-body and spin-exchange control inside the citation, because that adds a second storyline and weakens the narrow framing that you and Kroll both say is needed.

responses.point: The citation should be framed around the lattice concept and its realisation at 10^-18, and not pretend to adjudicate lattice versus ion clocks. Kroll also asks the committee to decide whether his doctoral stay in Hall's Boulder laboratory requires recusal for B036.
responses.response: This framing is what makes the 2012 overlap manageable, and I accept it. On the recusal question, a doctoral stay in a laboratory whose lineage connects to Ye's group, with no documented tie to Katori or Ye, looks to me like field proximity and not a conflict. I would want it disclosed in the record and left to the chair and the committee, and I would not want the discussion to turn on it. I also noted your fallback that B046 is the better place for atomic physics if the overlap proves decisive. I do not take that route, since B046 has five names for three places and I think the credit problem there is worse than for B036.

responses.point: B022 is a field-opening discovery that has been reproduced widely, the open question is the mechanism and not the existence of the effects, and a precision-measurement prize should not rank above a new phenomenon. Danielsson accepts B036 as a first alternative and would not oppose it.
responses.response: I agree that the effects in magic-angle graphene are real and reproduced, and I do not rank it third lightly. I still put maturity first this year. The pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder and the Yuan Cao gap in the credit are three open points, and the Cao gap is a credit problem of the same kind that made me abandon B054. I do not accept that a measurement-limited advance ranks below a new phenomenon as a matter of principle; the statutes say discovery or invention, and the lattice clock is a clear invention with scientific consequences. Your fallback to B036 means that our positions are closer than the rankings suggest.

responses.point: B054 is conceptually deep but Mehlig ranked it seventh because of the 2016 overlap and the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit. Mehlig leans to B022 over B036 but would accept B036 as a strong fallback if B022 is judged premature.
responses.response: You were right about both points on B054, and I have given up the configuration, though I still think the 2016 citation covered phase transitions and quantum Hall-type phases and not a symmetry-protected phase with time-reversal symmetry intact. As for B022, I take your point that the prize would rest on flat-band-driven correlated phases and not on a theory of the superconductivity. If the committee judges that the Cao gap and the maturity question can be answered, I would not stand in the way, which is why it is my second alternative. Your statement that B036 is an acceptable fallback is useful, because it means a B036 prize would not be a contested outcome for you.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on a citation drawn narrowly and on colleagues who know the field better than I do.
Whether two names are enough for B036 given the claims of Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto and the national-laboratory groups, and whether Ye's many-body work should be inside the citation.
Whether I am deferring too much to colleagues in atomic physics; my own judgement is limited here, and I am moving mainly because the specific objection I raised has been answered.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and none to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. I work in electronic-structure theory, which is far from atomic clocks. I chaired the 2025 cycle, which bears on the overlap argument for circuit QED (B044) but is not a personal conflict. I note Kroll's disclosure about the Hall laboratory and regard it as a matter for the committee to weigh.
